> - The "1% rule" isn't stated in any SR3 book checked, so it's been
>   removed.
> - "Astral Gateway collapse" isn't an SR3 hazard. **Focus addiction** is
>   real. *(MitS p.45)*
> - The Scenario C total was wrong: 8,000 × 3, then +100%, is **48,000¥**, not
>   32,000–40,000¥.
> - The **1,000¥ per point of Force** for hermetic conjuring materials was
>   correct. *(SR3 p.186; MitS p.169)*

pdf.quote: The summoning ritual also requires special ritual materials, available from a talismonger for approximately

entries.note: Errata callout. Focus addiction is a real MitS rule (printed p.45; the page's footer number is missing from its text layer so it cannot be recorded as evidence) and elemental conjuring materials cost about Force × 1,000¥ (SR3 p.186); neither is implemented. The Scenario C figure checks: 8,000 × 3 × 2 = 48,000.

entries.reason: page title / table of contents / heading / table header row / general description — states no rule

entries.text:
- **Drain**: casting above your Magic makes it **Physical**, and so does
  casting while astrally projecting. *(SR3 p.162)*

pdf.quote: If the Force of the spell is greater than the caster's Magic Attribute, the Drain causes physical damage
All spells cast while astrally projecting cause physical damage, regardless of Force

entries.text:
- **Magic loss**: on a Deadly wound, or medical treatment without the
  Awakened modifier, roll 2D6. At or under your Magic, you lose a point
  permanently. *(SR3 p.129)*

pdf.quote: The character's player rolls 2D6. If the result is less than or equal to the magician's current Magic Rating

entries.text:
- **Astral combat**: wounds taken on the astral appear on the body. Being
  disrupted forces a Magic Loss check. *(SR3 p.175)*
entries.reason: Astral damage appearing on the physical body and disruption forcing a Magic Loss check are on printed p.175, an image-only page (no text layer). Read via the SR-OCR dump: 'The physical body manifests any damage inflicted on the astral form' and 'A character who is disrupted in astral combat must immediately check for Magic Loss (p. 160)' — the guide agrees. The Magic Loss check for disruption is not implemented.

entries.text:
- **The law**: magic of **Force 3+** is regulated in the UCAS and CAS, and a
  felony committed with magic is treated as premeditated. *(MitS p.11)*
entries.reason: Legal background with no code counterpart. Checked against MitS printed p.11: Force 3+ magic is regulated in the UCAS and CAS, and a felony committed with magic is treated as premeditated; the guide agrees.

> - SR3 security codes are **Blue, Green, Orange and Red**, plus unofficial
>   "UV". There are no "Yellow" systems, and "Passive / Passive-Alert IC" is
>   not an IC type. *(SR3 p.205)*
> - **Blaster, sparky and tar pit are gray IC**: they damage the deck and its
>   programs. **Black IC** is the kind that hurts the decker, including the
>   psychotropic variety. *(SR3 p.227–230)*
> - The "Scenario C" total was right. The others are restated below with the
>   formula from [the hiring overview](../#the-house-rule-framework).

pdf.quote: Green (average security), Orange (significant security), and Red (high security)
the decker must spend a Complex Action and make a successful Willpower (Black IC Rating) Test to jack out

entries.note: Errata callout. Security codes Blue/Green/Orange/Red plus unofficial 'UV' (printed p.205) is implemented for the Orthodox host sheet; blaster, sparky and tar pit are gray IC and black IC hurts the decker (pp.227-230) is not (the Orthodox IC sheet has no Tar Pit type and no black-IC handling — see rules/combat.md #146, #147).

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> - There's no adept power called "Authoritative Voice". The SR3 powers are
>   **Commanding Voice** and **Kinesics**. *(SOTA64 p.64–66)*
> - A Rating 4–6 fake ID doesn't cost "1,000–10,000¥". By the Creating a
>   Credstick Table it's **16,000¥ at Rating 4 and 30,000¥ at Rating 6**.
>   *(SR3 p.239)*
> - *Corporate Download* is a real SR3 book, but it isn't in the library used
>   for checking. Nothing on this page depends on it.
entries.reason: Composite errata callout. Commanding Voice (SOTA64 p.64-65) and Kinesics (p.66) exist and 'Authoritative Voice' is absent from the core text; a Rating 4 fake ID costs 16,000¥ and Rating 6 costs 30,000¥ by the Creating a Credstick Table (p.239, agrees); Corporate Download is not in the library. Fake IDs are not modelled in the system.

entries.text: ## The house-rule framework
entries.reason: page title / description / table of contents / heading / table header / horizontal rule / index or method text — states no game rule

entries.text:
{: .house }
> The specialist pages use this structure. It came from the original gists.
> The numbers are **not from any SR3 book**, and are **much higher** than the
> Companion's baselines. For example, a "professional" bodyguard at
> 1,500¥ a night compares with the book's **200¥ a day**. They fit a
> high-paying campaign. Scale them to your table.
entries.reason: House-rule framework (the guide marks it as not from any SR3 book)

entries.text:
**Fee = base day rate × threat multiplier, plus hazard pay (a percentage of
that), plus expenses.**
entries.reason: House-rule framework (the guide marks it as not from any SR3 book)

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> - The power is **Improved Reflexes** (levels 1–3, +1D6 to +3D6 Initiative),
>   not "Increased Reflexes". Its bonus **can't be combined** with wired
>   reflexes or other technological or magical boosts. *(SR3 p.169)*
> - Initiative dice aren't Initiative Passes. The number of passes comes from
>   the Initiative score, which drops by 10 each pass. *(SR3 p.104)*
> - There are no adept powers called "Invisibility" or "Silence". For stealth,
>   look at **Traceless Walk** *(MitS p.151)* and **Melanin Control**
>   *(SOTA64 p.67–68)*.
> - "Wall-walking" is **Wall Running**. "Bushido / Way powers" isn't an SR3
>   term, so it's been removed.
> - The Scenario C total was wrong: 18,000 × 4, then +50%, is **108,000¥**,
>   not 81,000¥.
entries.reason: Composite errata callout. Improved Reflexes (levels 1-3) not combining with technological or magical boosts (SR3 p.169) is implemented (SR3EActor.reflexBonus); initiative passes dropping 10 a pass (p.104) is implemented; Traceless Walk (MitS p.151), Melanin Control (SOTA64 p.67) and Wall Running (SOTA64 p.68) exist at the cited pages; 'Invisibility' and 'Silence' are spells, not adept powers, in the core rulebook. The Scenario C figure checks: 18,000 × 4 × 1.5 = 108,000.

{: .no_toc }
entries.reason: page title / table of contents / heading / table header row / general description — states no rule

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> - Shamans summon **nature spirits** of **Man, Land, Sky and Waters**, not
>   "domain spirits". They can only summon inside the spirit's domain, and a
>   nature spirit **can't leave its domain**. *(SR3 p.184, p.266–267)*
> - A spirit gives **one service per success** on the Conjuring Test, and
>   nature spirits **vanish at sunrise and sunset**. So "bring pre-summoned
>   spirits to the job" has a hard time limit. *(SR3 p.186)*
> - The Scenario C total was wrong: 8,000 × 3, then +50% and +100%, is
>   **60,000¥**, not 36,000–44,000¥.

pdf.quote: There are four classes of nature spirits
Nature spirits vanish at sunrise and sunset, no matter what

entries.note: Errata callout. Nature spirits come in four classes (Man, Land, Sky, Waters — printed p.266), can be summoned only in the spirit's domain (p.184) and vanish at sunrise and sunset (p.186), one service per Conjuring success (p.186). The system has some of the spirit types but does not enforce the domain or the sunrise/sunset limit (see magic/awakened-primer.md #21, #23). The Scenario C figure checks: 8,000 × 3 × (1 + .5 + 1) = 60,000.

code.snippet: for (let score = base; score > 0; score -= 10, pass++)

entries.note: Errata callout. Wired reflexes give +2/+4/+6 Reaction and +1D6/+2D6/+3D6 Initiative, not extra passes (printed p.104, p.301); the passes come from the score dropping by 10 each pass. The Scenario B and C totals check: 5,000 × 2 × 1.5 = 15,000 and 7,000 × 4 × 1.5 = 42,000.

# Primer for the Awakened
{: .no_toc }
entries.reason: page title / description / table of contents / horizontal rule / index page

entries.text:
What a starting magician can do, how astral space works, and what an elven
mage in Seattle knows about the world.
entries.reason: page title / description / table of contents / horizontal rule / index page

entries.text:
1. TOC

entries.reason: page title / description / table of contents / horizontal rule / index page

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> Original gist: "Primer for the Awakened Elf".
> - Drain codes like "4L, 3M, 5H" don't exist. SR3 writes Drain as `+1(M)`,
>   meaning Power = Force ÷ 2 + 1 at Moderate. There is no "H" level.
> - Force is capped by **the Force you learned the spell at**, not by your
>   Magic. Casting above your Magic is legal; the Drain just becomes Physical.
> - Nature spirits come in **four** families: Man, Land, Sky and Waters.
>   "Aura Masking" is not a spirit service.
> - SR3 ritual sorcery uses a **material link**. "Sympathetic link" is a term
>   from a later edition.
> - Astral attacks use an **Astral Combat Pool** and Sorcery, Unarmed Combat
>   or an armed skill with a weapon focus. The gist's "Astral Combat + Combat
>   Pool" was wrong. **Force / Magic is not astral armor.**
> - Projecting movement: normal speed is **Intelligence × 4 m per turn**, and
>   fast movement is up to **Magic in kilometers per turn**, not a flat
>   100 km per turn.
> - The Awakening is dated **24 December 2011**, when the dragon Ryumyo
>   appeared near Mount Fuji. It was not 21 December.

pdf.quote: Projecting characters and spirits have an Astral Combat Pool equal to the sum of their Mental Attributes, divided by two and rounded down
Fast movement is very fast! Your astral form can move up to a number of kilometers equal to your Magic Attribute in a single turn
There are four classes of nature spirits

entries.note: Composite errata callout. Checked against the book: Drain written +1(M) (p.191) and no 'H' level; Force capped by the Force learned (p.178) with Physical Drain above Magic (p.183); four nature-spirit classes Man/Land/Sky/Waters (p.266); material link in ritual sorcery (MitS); astral combat uses the Astral Combat Pool (p.174); projecting movement Intelligence x 4 m and Magic km per turn (p.173); Ryumyo seen on 24 December 2011 (p.25, p.269).

pdf.quote: There are five categories: Combat, Detection, Health, Illusion and Manipulation spells

  or lower, never higher. *(SR3 p.178)* At character creation no spell can
  be bought above Force 6. *(SR3 p.60)*

pdf.quote: can never cast the spell at a higher Force than they have learned

entries.note: The character-creation limit (no spell above Force 6, p.60) is not enforced -- chargen is not automated.

- **Casting** is a Complex Action: roll **Sorcery** plus up to as many
  **Spell Pool** dice as Sorcery dice. The TN is the target's **Willpower**
  (mana spells) or **Body** (physical spells), or its Object Resistance.

entries.note: Same two gaps as magic/spellcasting.md #7 and #43: the Spell Pool cap ('no more pool dice than Sorcery dice') and the Object Resistance Table are not implemented. Casting itself is a Complex Action and the Willpower/Body target numbers are.

entries.text:

  the Damage Level shown. Resist with **Willpower** plus any number of Spell
  Pool dice, and reduce one level per 2 successes. *(SR3 p.162, p.44)*

## Step 1: Preparation  *(SR3 p.178, p.181, p.191)*

entries.text:
- **The spell and its Force.** You can cast at the Force you learned it at
  or lower, never higher. The minimum is Force 1. *(SR3 p.178)* Higher Force
  is harder to resist and produces more Drain.

pdf.quote: can never cast the spell at a higher Force than they have learned. The minimum Force for any spell is 1
The higher the Force of a spell, the greater its potential effect and the harder it is for the target to resist

entries.text:
- **Damage Level, for combat and elemental spells.** You choose **L, M, S or
  D** when you cast. That choice is both the spell's base damage **and** its
  base Drain Level. *(SR3 p.191, p.196)*

pdf.quote: The caster chooses the spell's Base Damage Level when it is cast, which also determines the base Drain Level

entries.text:
- **How many Sorcery dice** go into this spell, and how many **Spell Pool**
  dice. You can't add more pool dice than Sorcery dice. *(SR3 p.180)*

pdf.quote: No more Spell Pool dice can be used than the number of Sorcery dice allocated to the test

entries.text:
- **More than one spell?** You can split Sorcery and Spell Pool dice to cast
  several spells in one Complex Action, up to your Sorcery rating in spells,
  with at least 1 Sorcery die each. Each spell then gets **+2 to its Drain
  TN for every extra spell**. Two spells means +2 on each Drain Test; three
  means +4 on each. *(SR3 p.181)*

pdf.quote: The caster receives a +2 target number modifier for each extra spell to the Drain Resistance Test for all of the spells

entries.note: The system casts one spell per Complex Action. Splitting Sorcery and Spell Pool dice across several spells, the Sorcery-rating limit on how many, and the +2 Drain TN per extra spell do not exist.

entries.text:
- **Sustaining anything?** Choose whether to keep or drop spells you're
  already sustaining. Each one you keep costs **+2 to all your tests**,
  including this Sorcery Test and its Drain Test. *(SR3 p.178)*

pdf.quote: Characters sustaining spells have a +2 target modifier per sustained spell applied to all tests, including Drain Resistance Tests

entries.text:
- **Area spells**: the base radius is your **Magic in meters**, and it hits
  everyone valid inside, **including you and your friends**. Withhold
  Sorcery dice to change it: **every 2 dice withheld shrink it by 1 m**, or
  **every 1 die withheld widens it by 1 m**. *(SR3 p.181)*

pdf.quote: Area spells affect all valid targets within the radius of effect, friend and foe alike (including the caster)
every die withheld from the Sorcery Test increases the radius by 1 meter

entries.note: Fixed for 0.6.1 (TODO 171). The caster is now included (_actorsInRadius no longer filters a.id === caster.id), and the radius is computed from withheld Sorcery dice via spellAreaRadius (narrow: 1m per 2 dice withheld; widen: 1m per die withheld), read at cast time.

{: #step-2-targeting }

pdf.quote: the caster must be able to see the target and must be present on the same plane

entries.text:
- You must **see** the target, and be **on the same plane** (physical or
  astral). Glasses, mirrors, fiber optics and cybereyes are fine. **Any
  digital image**, such as a camera feed, simsense or a vision-altering spell
  like Clairvoyance, is not. *(SR3 p.181)*

pdf.quote: An opaque barrier prevents the caster from seeing the target
prevents the caster from casting spells on that target

entries.note: Line of sight, plane, glass and opaque barriers are the GM's call: targets are picked from a list or found by radius, with no sight or barrier check.

prevents the caster from casting spells on that target

entries.note: Line of sight, plane, glass and opaque barriers are the GM's call: targets are picked from a list or found by radius, with no sight or barrier check.

pdf.quote: One net success is sufficient for the caster to touch the target
Spells with a range of touch are not subject to cover or visibility modifiers

## Step 4: Spell Resistance  *(SR3 p.183)*
{: #step-4-spell-resistance }

pdf.quote: Living targets may always make a Spell Resistance Test

entries.text:
Two different things can reduce the caster's successes here. Both can happen
against the same spell.
entries.reason: introductory sentence; the two mechanisms it announces (target resists, spell defense) are checked in the units below

entries.text: ### The target resists
entries.reason: section heading

entries.text:
- Any **living** target that isn't **willing** makes a **Spell Resistance
  Test**: its **targeted attribute** (usually Body, Intelligence or
  Willpower) against **TN = the spell's Force**.

pdf.quote: Living targets may always make a Spell Resistance Test against spells, unless the target of the spell is willing

entries.note: A resistance test is offered to every live target; the exception for a willing target ('unless the target of the spell is willing') is not modelled.

entries.text:
- **No modifiers apply** unless the spell says so. That includes the
  target's wounds. *(SR3 p.183)*

pdf.quote: No target modifiers apply to this test except where specifically noted

entries.text: - **Non-living, non-magical** targets don't resist.

pdf.quote: Non-living, non-magical targets may not make a Resistance Test

entries.text:
> **How The 2nd Chumming reads it:** a target who is **sustaining spells**
> still takes **+2 per spell** on this test. The book says both "no target
> modifiers apply to this test" *(SR3 p.183)* and that sustaining costs +2 on
> "all tests, including Drain Resistance Tests (but not normal Damage
> Resistance Tests)" *(SR3 p.178)*. The maintainer ruled that p.178's "all
> tests" wins (2026-09-14). Wounds still don't apply.
{: .house }

pdf.quote: No target modifiers apply to this test except where specifically noted
Characters sustaining spells have a +2 target modifier per sustained spell applied to all tests, including Drain Resistance Tests (but not normal Damage Resistance Tests)

entries.note: House-rule callout documenting the maintainer's 2026-09-14 ruling that resolves a real conflict between p.178 ('all tests') and p.183 ('no target modifiers except where noted'): handleSpellResistRoll sets skipWoundMod but not skipSustainMod, so rollPool applies the sustaining +2 to the Spell Resistance Test while wounds are excluded, matching the stated ruling.

entries.text: ### A magician blocks it: Spell Defense  *(SR3 p.183)*

pdf.quote: Sorcery can be used to defend against the effects of spells as well as cast them

entries.text:
- At some earlier point, a magician **set aside Sorcery and Spell Pool dice
  for defense**. That's a Free Action.

pdf.quote: Allocating Spell Defense dice is a Free Action

entries.text:
- They can protect up to **their Sorcery rating** in subjects, all within
  **Magic × 100 m** and on the same plane. Protecting yourself counts as one.

pdf.quote: within a distance equal to the caster's Magic Attribute x 100 meters, can be protected
A character can protect a maximum number of subjects equal to their Sorcery Skill Rating

entries.note: A mage's Spell Defense pool is one total for the Combat Turn. Who is protected, the Sorcery-rating limit on subjects, the Magic × 100 m range and the same-plane condition are not recorded; every defender with a pool is offered a Counterspelling roll against any spell.

entries.text:
- When a protected subject is targeted, the defender **senses it** and may
  roll any of those dice against **TN = the spell's Force**. It takes no
  action.

pdf.quote: Any Spell Defense dice the magician wishes to use are rolled against a target number equal to the Force of the spell

code.snippet: state._pendingDefenseCard = { currentSuccesses: bestHits, sc, force: sc.force };

entries.text:
- **Every success subtracts one success from the caster's Sorcery Test.** If
  that takes the caster to **0 or less**, the spell fails.

pdf.quote: Any successes subtract directly from the successes the spell's caster achieves on the Sorcery Test

entries.text: - Dice used are **gone until the next Combat Turn**.

pdf.quote: Once used, Spell Defense dice are lost until the magician's next Combat Turn

code.snippet: turn; Sorcery dice return at round end.

## Step 5: Spell Effect  *(SR3 p.183, p.191)*
{: #step-5-spell-effect }

pdf.quote: If the target generated the same number or more successes, the spell does not affect the target

entries.text:
Compare the caster's remaining successes with the target's resistance
successes.

pdf.quote: the caster's successes are compared to the successes generated by the target

entries.text: - **Target ties or wins:** **no effect.** A tie goes to the target.

pdf.quote: If the target generated the same number or more successes, the spell does not affect the target

entries.text:
- **Caster wins:** the **net successes** (caster − target) measure the
  effect. The spell's description says what they buy.

pdf.quote: The spell's effect is measured as the difference between the caster's successes and the target's

entries.text:
- **No resistance roll** (an object, or a willing subject): all the caster's
  successes count, and **1 success always gives some effect**.

pdf.quote: When casting spells against non-resisting targets (which are generally non-living targets) one success always insures some degree of effect

entries.text:
- **Damaging spells:** the chosen Damage Level **stages up one level per 2
  net successes**, up to Deadly.

pdf.quote: For any spells that damage the target, stage up the Damage Level for every 2 net successes

entries.text: ### Combat spells: armor doesn't help  *(SR3 p.191)*

pdf.quote: Combat spells ignore the effects of armor and nonmagical, external protections

code.snippet: //   Net successes (caster − resister) stage the base damage. No soak.

entries.text:
Combat spells (Manabolt, Powerbolt, Stunbolt and their ball versions)
damage the target **directly and bypass armor**. The Spell Resistance Test
is the target's only defense, so **there's no Damage Resistance Test**.
Mana spells are resisted with **Willpower** and affect only living and
magical targets. Physical spells are resisted with **Body** and can hit
objects too.

pdf.quote: Combat spells ignore the effects of armor and nonmagical, external protections
Only physical spells affect non-living objects

code.snippet: //   Net successes (caster − resister) stage the base damage. No soak.

entries.text:
Fireball, Flamethrower, Lightning Bolt, Acid Stream and similar spells make

guard with Willpower **4**. She isn't sustaining anything.

{: .fixed }
> Original gist: "Complete Actions & Combat System Guide".
> - You get **one Free Action in every Combat Phase**, including other
>   characters' phases, not one per Initiative Pass.
> - "Take Cover" is not an SR3 action. "Suppressive fire" is not a defined
>   action or modifier in the core rules; the phrase appears only in a rigger
>   example (SR3 p.156).
> - Nearly every value in the modifiers table was wrong: partial cover is
>   **+4**, target running is **+2**, and the visibility values come from a
>   two-axis table.
> - Damage staging is **net**: attacker successes are compared with the
>   defender's Dodge + Damage Resistance successes. The dodge doesn't reduce
>   the attacker's successes directly.
> - SR3 has a **Spell Pool**, not a Magic Pool. Drain TN is Force ÷ 2 plus a
>   modifier; there is no minimum-2 rule of its own.
> - Matrix: there is no "Access Node" action (the nearest is the **Locate
>   Access Node** operation, SR3 p.210) and no "Response Index". Hacking Pool
>   **cannot** be used to resist black IC.
> - Vehicles: "VCTR" is not an SR3 term. A crash test comes from **Serious**
>   damage in one attack, not Moderate, and the TN is Handling.

{: #spellcasting-and-drain }
entries.reason: section heading

The full step-by-step, with Spell Defense, elemental spells and sustaining, is
on [Spellcasting, Resistance & Drain](../../magic/spellcasting/).
entries.reason: cross-reference to another guide page

entries.text: Casting a spell is a **Complex Action**. *(SR3 p.107)*

pdf.quote: A magician may cast a spell by taking a Complex Action

entries.text:
1. **Force**: you can cast a spell at any Force up to the one you learned it
   at, never higher. *(SR3 p.178)*

pdf.quote: can never cast the spell at a higher Force than they have learned

entries.text:
2. **Sorcery Test**: Sorcery dice plus up to an equal number of **Spell
   Pool** dice. The TN is the target's **Willpower** for mana spells or
   **Body** for physical spells. Objects use the Object Resistance Table:
   natural 3, low-tech 5, high-tech 8, highly processed 10+. *(SR3 p.182)*
   If every die shows 1, the spell fails and Drain TN rises by 2.
   *(SR3 p.182)*

pdf.quote: No more Spell Pool dice can be added to the test than the Sorcery dice allocated
Consult the Object Resistance Table for examples of objects and materials

entries.note: Implemented from this unit: the Sorcery Test against the target's Willpower (mana) or Body (physical), and the all-ones glitch adding +2 to the Drain TN (SR3EActor.js:9730). Not implemented: (1) the Object Resistance Table — there is no way to target an object and no object target numbers (natural 3, low-tech 5, high-tech 8, processed 10+); (2) the cap 'no more Spell Pool dice than Sorcery dice allocated' — the prompt offers everything available (SR3EItem.js:4548-4568, `_promptMagicPool(actor, availMagic)`).

entries.text:
3. **Resistance**: the target resists with the same attribute, and the net
   successes decide the effect.

pdf.quote: The target makes a Resistance Test using the targeted Attribute (usually Body, Intelligence or Willpower)

code.snippet: return { tn: Math.max(2, val), resistAttr: attr, resistName: name, attrLabel: name };

entries.text:
4. **Drain**: every spell lists a code like `+1(M)`. Drain **Power** (the TN)
   = **Force ÷ 2, rounded down, + the modifier**; **M** is the Damage
   Level. Resist with **Willpower** plus any number of Spell Pool dice.
   Every 2 successes reduce the level one step. *(SR3 p.162, p.44)*

pdf.quote: The target number is the Force of the spell, divided by 2 (rounded down) plus any Drain Modifier
Every two successes generated in the Drain Resistance Test lowers the Drain Level by one level

code.snippet: return { tn: Math.max(2, halfF + powerMod + abovePower), level };

     Magic, or if you are astrally projecting. *(SR3 p.162)*

pdf.quote: Charisma to resist Conjuring Drain

entries.reason: section heading

entries.text:
- **Hacking Pool** = (Intelligence + MPCP) ÷ 3, rounded down. You can add at
  most your skill dice from it to a test. It **can't** be used on Body or
  Willpower tests against gray or black IC, or on Etiquette (Matrix).
  *(SR3 p.44)*

pdf.quote: Hacking Pool dice cannot be used in Body or Willpower Tests to resist the effects of gray or black ice
Hacking Pool also may not be used with Etiquette (Matrix) Tests
The maximum number of Hacking Pool dice that can be added to any test is equal to the base number of skill dice in use

entries.note: The formula is implemented (SR3EActor.js:2304, and the Orthodox equivalent). Not implemented: (1) the cap 'the maximum number of Hacking Pool dice that can be added to any test is equal to the base number of skill dice' — the pool prompts offer everything available (only defaulting caps it); (2) the prohibition on Hacking Pool for Body / Willpower resistance against gray or black IC (no IC damage resistance flow exists for the Orthodox ruleset); (3) the prohibition on Etiquette (Matrix) tests.

entries.text:
- **Matrix Initiative**: your persona's Reaction + **1D6**. Each point of
  **Response Increase** adds +2 Reaction and **+1D6**, up to 3 points and no
  more than MPCP ÷ 4. Wired reflexes and other physical boosts don't apply.
  *(SR3 p.207, p.223)*

pdf.quote: Each point of Response Increase increases a persona's Reaction Attribute by 2 and Initiative by +1D6
Response Increase cannot exceed a deck's MPCP Rating divided by 4
Wired reflexes, magical augmentation, vehicle-control rigs, and other enhancements that increase the Reaction Attribute

entries.note: The '+2 Reaction and +1D6 per point, up to 3 and MPCP÷4' limits are shown as a tooltip on the Response field, not enforced (SR3EActorSheet.js:2270).

entries.text: - Icons get the same Free / Simple / Complex actions. *(SR3 p.223)*

pdf.quote: An icon may take one Free Action, and either two Simple Actions or one Complex Action during a Combat Phase

entries.note: The Matrix has no actions of its own in the ledger; icons in the tracker use the same generic ledger the GM marks by hand.

entries.text:
- **System Tests**: you roll Computer against the relevant subsystem rating
  (Access, Control, Index, Files, Slave). The host rolls its Security Value
  against your Detection Factor, and its successes build your **security
  tally**, which triggers alerts and IC. *(SR3 p.209–210)*

pdf.quote: the host/grid rolls makes a Security Test, rolling its Security Value against a target number equal to the decker's Detection Factor
target number when making tests to detect a decker's presence

entries.text:
- **Security codes**: Blue, Green, Orange, Red. Deckers call the ones off
  the chart "UV". *(SR3 p.205)*

pdf.quote: Green (average security), Orange (significant security), and Red (high security)
The following section details various forms of white, gray, and black IC

entries.text:
- **White** affects only your icon: crippler, killer, probe, scramble,
    tar baby.

pdf.quote: White IC affects only the decker's on-
Scramble IC is reactive IC used to protect elements of a

entries.text:
- **Gray** attacks your deck and utilities: blaster, ripper, sparky, tar
    pit.

pdf.quote: Gray IC programs attack a decker's cyberdeck and utilities
The reactive IC known as tar pit IC operates and attacks in

entries.note: Tar pit is a gray IC in the book (printed p.229) but the Orthodox IC sheet's type list has no 'Tar Pit' (Probe, Trace, Blaster, Crippler, Tar Baby, Scramble, Killer, Ripper, Marker, Sparky). Blaster, ripper and sparky are present.

entries.text:
- **Black** attacks **you**. Against lethal black IC you resist with
    **Body**, reduced by Hardening. Hacking Pool can't be used; Karma Pool
    can. After black IC hits you, jacking out takes a Complex Action and a
    Willpower (IC Rating) Test. *(SR3 p.230)*

pdf.quote: the decker must spend a Complex Action and make a successful Willpower (Black IC Rating) Test to jack out
Hardening reduces the Power of the damage for these Resistance Tests
The Hacking Pool may not be used for this test, though Karma Pool dice may be

entries.note: No black-IC handling exists in the Orthodox flow: no lethal/non-lethal distinction, no Body resistance reduced by Hardening (the Hardening field is on the sheet but read by no roll), no Hacking Pool prohibition, and no jack-out Complex Action with a Willpower (IC Rating) Test after a black-IC hit.

- **Tortoises** (cyberterminals) can't be hurt by black IC or dump shock.
  *(SR3 p.208)*

pdf.quote: tortoise users cannot be hurt by black IC or dump shock

  and **hot ASIST**, which you need for Response Increase and Hacking Pool.

entries.text: ## Vehicle combat & rigging  *(summary)*
entries.reason: section heading

entries.text:
- **Vehicle Control Rig**: each level gives +2 Reaction and **+1D6**
  Initiative while rigging. *(SR3 p.301)*

pdf.quote: Each level adds +2 to the user's Reaction and +1D6 Initiative dice while rigging

code.snippet: const base = Rigging.vcrReaction(reactionBase, vcrLevel) + wm - jam;

entries.note: Fixed for 0.6.1 (TODO 167). scripts/data/rigging.mjs's Rigging.vcrReaction/vcrInitiativeDice give +2 Reaction and +1 initiative die per VCR level, and both the rigger's own and the jumped-in vehicle's initiative call it (SR3EActor.js:10052, 10170).

entries.text:
- **Control Pool** = Reaction as modified by the VCR. *(SR3 p.44)* It only
  works in a vehicle adapted for rigger control. *(SR3 p.134)*

pdf.quote: A rigger's Control Pool is equal to the character's Reaction, modified only by his or her vehicle control rig
the vehicle is adapted for rigger control

entries.note: Fixed for 0.6.1 (TODO 167). Rigging.controlPool now returns Reaction (base) + 2 x VCR level, 0 without a VCR, and every site (gunnery, Driving Test, chase) reads it through Rigging.controlPool/controlPoolDice rather than the Vehicle Skill rating. The 'adapted for rigger control' precondition is still not modelled as its own field.

entries.text:
- **Driving Tests** use the vehicle's **Handling** as base TN. A jacked-in
  rigger subtracts the VCR rating. Vehicle-combat maneuver tables subtract
  **2 × VCR rating**. *(SR3 p.134, p.142–144)*

pdf.quote: reduce the target number by an amount equal to the VCR Rating
reduce the target number by an amount equal to twice the rigger's VCR Rating

entries.text:
- **Gunnery**: mounted weapons use the Gunnery skill and the ordinary
  ranged-combat rules. Sensor-enhanced gunnery adds half the Sensor rating
  in dice. *(SR3 p.151–152)*

pdf.quote: The player rolls a number of dice equal to the character's Gunnery Skill plus half the vehicle's Sensor Rating (round down)
all standard ranged combat rules apply

entries.note: Fixed for 0.6.1 (TODO 168). Sensor-enhanced gunnery now adds half the Sensor Rating (round down) as DICE via sensorGunneryDice, folded into the pool, with the TN set from the target's Signature (defaultTN = Math.max(2, baseSig)).

entries.text:
- **Shooting a vehicle**: halve the weapon's Power and drop its Damage Level
  one step, then subtract vehicle armor. If what's left doesn't beat the
  armor, no damage. Anti-vehicle munitions skip the halving and subtract
  only half the armor. *(SR3 p.149)*

pdf.quote: Weapons that do Light Damage cannot affect the vehicle unless the attacker uses special ammunition
The Power of the AV munitions is reduced by half the Armor Rating

entries.note: Fixed for 0.6.1 (TODO 168). vehicleTargetDamage now rounds Power down (Math.floor), flags Light damage as noEffect instead of mapping L to L, and AV munitions skip the halving/level-drop and instead halve the vehicle's armour at the soak card (SR3EActor.js:8462-8467).

entries.text:
- **Vehicle Damage Resistance**: vehicle Body plus Control Pool dice up to
  the Driving skill, against the modified Power. Riggers may **dodge** with
  Control Pool against the vehicle's Handling. *(SR3 p.149)*

pdf.quote: plus any available Control Pool dice up to the character's Driving Skill Rating
Riggers may attempt to dodge any ranged combat attack using Control Pool instead of Combat Pool dice

entries.note: A vehicle target rolls no Control Pool dice on its Damage Resistance Test (the soak card's pool is forced to 0 for vehicles, SR3EActor.js:8300) and vehicles never dodge, so a rigger's Control Pool dodge against Handling does not exist.

entries.text:
- **Crash Tests** are required when a vehicle takes **Serious** damage in a
  single attack, reaches Destroyed, takes damage from a ram, or brakes harder
  than Acceleration × 4. The test is a Driving Test against **Handling**.
  *(SR3 p.147)*

pdf.quote: Vehicle takes Serious damage in a single attack (including weapon and spell attacks)
The Crash Test consists of a Driving Test against a base target number equal to the vehicle's Handling Rating

entries.note: The Crash Test itself (a Driving Test against Handling with the Crash Test Modifiers Table) is implemented. Whether one is required is the GM's reading of the scene — no trigger fires automatically.

entries.text:
- **Rigger damage**: if the vehicle takes Serious damage, the jacked-in
  rigger resists **6M** Physical. If it's destroyed, **6S**. This is resisted
  with **Willpower**, and no pool dice can be used. *(SR3 p.145)*

pdf.quote: the controlling rigger must make a Damage Resistance Test against 6M Physical damage

# Decking (Matrix Defragged)

entries.reason: page title

entries.text:
This table plays **Matrix Defragged v2**, a fan-made replacement for the core rulebook's Matrix
chapter (SR3 p.199–232). It isn't an official Shadowrun supplement — it's a fan rewrite by
Brinoceros, built to run faster at the table — but it's cited here the same way as any other
sourcebook: `*(MDF p.NN)*`, printed page.

pdf.quote: This section walks users through the basic process

entries.note: Introduction: names the book and its citation style.

entries.text:
This system can run either ruleset — Defragged or the core rulebook's own Matrix chapter,
"Orthodox SR3" — as a per-world setting. If your table runs Orthodox instead, see
[Decking (SR3 core)](../decking/). The two rulesets don't mix; this page covers Defragged only.

entries.text: ### Choosing the ruleset
entries.reason: heading

entries.text:
A world setting, **Matrix Ruleset** (under Foundry's Configure Settings), switches between
**"Matrix Defragged v2"** (the default, described on this page) and **"Orthodox SR3 Matrix"**.
Changing it needs a full Foundry restart, and the GM sees a warning that switching mid-campaign
could break things — this is a session-zero decision, not a mid-run one.
entries.reason: describes the system's interface, not a book rule

entries.text: ### Getting on the Matrix
entries.reason: heading

entries.text: On the **Matrix** tab of a character or NPC sheet:
entries.reason: describes the system's interface, not a book rule

entries.text:
- **User Mode buttons** — `TRM`, `AR`, `VR-Cold`, `VR-Hot` — set your Matrix mode. Clicking one
  opens an "Enter Matrix" dialog to pick which **host actor** you're connecting to; confirming
  sets both the mode and your active host. Clicking the same mode again disconnects you and
  drops you from that host's roster. Switching into either VR mode while driving a vehicle in
  rigger-control mode automatically kicks the vehicle back to remote control, since the two are
  mutually exclusive.
entries.reason: describes the system's interface, not a book rule

entries.text:
- **Cyberdecks** are items in your inventory. The Matrix tab lists yours (name, MPCP, Firewall,
  Response) with an **Equip** toggle. The equipped deck shows its full stat block — MPCP,
  Firewall, Response, memory used/total, free utility slots, transfer rate, Flux rating, your
  Hacking Pool bonus, and your Matrix Initiative — plus its own 10-box Matrix condition track.
entries.reason: describes the system's interface, not a book rule

entries.text:
- **Programs** are also items; drag one onto a numbered utility slot on your deck to load it. A
  slot can be marked **burned** if an attack knocks it out, or ejected to swap the program out.
  Loaded programs are rolled straight from their slot (hold Shift for physical dice).
entries.reason: describes the system's interface, not a book rule

entries.text:
A **Cybercombat** button lets you target anyone sharing your host connection — other connected
deckers, deployed IC, or agents — and posts a two-sided card for the exchange. Each side's own

# Decking (SR3 core)
{: .no_toc }
entries.reason: page title

entries.text:
This page covers the **core rulebook's own Matrix chapter** (SR3 p.199–232), plus the hot/cold
ASIST rules from the *Matrix* sourcebook. This system calls this ruleset **"Orthodox SR3 Matrix"**
to distinguish it from **Matrix Defragged**, a fan-made simplified ruleset this table can run
instead — see [Decking (Matrix Defragged)](../decking-defragged/) if that's what your GM chose.
The two rulesets are mechanically incompatible; this page only covers Orthodox.

pdf.quote: The MPCP Rating is the central value for cyberdecks. The

entries.text: ## The pieces
entries.reason: heading

entries.text:
A decker's **cyberdeck** defines everything about their persona in the Matrix. Its central
number is the **MPCP Rating** — think of it as the deck's overall processing muscle. Three times
the MPCP Rating is the total the decker can spread across four **persona programs**: **Bod**,
**Evasion**, **Masking**, and **Sensor**, none of which can individually exceed the MPCP itself.
These four act as the persona's "attributes" whenever something in the Matrix tests against the
decker directly. *(SR3 p.206)*

pdf.quote: MPCP Rating multiplied by 3 equals the maximum total of the
exceed the MPCP Rating, and the maximum value for utility

entries.note: The sheet warns when the persona total exceeds MPCP × 3; it does not flag a single program above MPCP (see #112).

entries.text:
A deck also carries **Hardening**, which blunts damage from the nastiest IC; **Active** and
**Storage Memory**, which limit how many utility programs can run at once versus just be carried;
an **I/O Speed** for moving data; and **Response Increase**, the Matrix's answer to wired
reflexes — each point adds +2 to Reaction and +1D6 to Matrix Initiative. A deck supports at most
3 points, and no more than its MPCP ÷ 4 (round down), so a deck of MPCP 3 or less can't run any.
*(SR3 p.206–207)*

pdf.quote: MPCP Rating divided by 4, rounding fractions down (so a
A deck can support only 3 points of Response Increase.

entries.note: Guide corrected in 0.6.3 (e06c95f7); it was guide-differs in this check. The sheet warns above MPCP ÷ 4, which is never more than 3 for a deck of MPCP 12 or less.

entries.text:
Most ordinary Matrix users aren't running a full cyberdeck at all — they're on a **cyberterminal**
("tortoise" in decker slang), a cheaper, weaker rig capped at a low MPCP. The upside: tortoise
users can't be hurt by black IC or Dumpshock. *(SR3 p.207–208)*

pdf.quote: positive side, tortoise users cannot be hurt by black IC or dump

entries.text:
Outside combat, a decker's number of actions per turn comes from their Reaction divided by 10
(rounded up), plus one extra action per bonus Initiative die from Response Increase. In
cybercombat, it works like ordinary SR3 Initiative: base Reaction plus 1D6, with each point of
Response Increase adding +2 Reaction and another die. Reflex boosts that only affect the physical
body — wired reflexes, magic, vehicle rigs — don't carry over into the Matrix. Staying in live
voice or text contact with the outside world while decking costs a die of Initiative.

entries.text: ## Hosts, grids, and getting in
entries.reason: heading

entries.text:
Every host or grid carries an overall **Security Rating** — a colour code plus a number — and
five **subsystem ratings**: **Access**, **Control**, **Index**, **Files**, and **Slave**. Each
subsystem is the TN for a specific kind of illegitimate action against it: getting in at all uses
Access, kicking a user off or reprogramming something uses Control, searching for data uses
Index, reading or writing files uses Files, and operating a connected physical device (a camera, a
maglock) uses Slave. *(SR3 p.205–206)*

pdf.quote: Rating and five subsystem ratings--Access, Control, Index,

entries.text:
The colour code — **Blue** (barely any security), **Green** (average), **Orange** (a system worth
protecting), or **Red** (the kind that shoots first) — gives a rough sense of what to expect
before a decker even rolls anything, and unofficially there's a level above Red that deckers call
"Ultra-Violet." *(SR3 p.205)*

pdf.quote: The four security codes are Blue (little or no security), Green
slang calls these Ultra-Violet, UV, or black systems.

entries.text:
A **System Test** is always a Success Contest: the decker's Computer skill (plus any Hacking Pool
committed) against the relevant subsystem rating, opposed by the host's own Security Value rolled
against the decker's **Detection Factor** — the average of their Masking Rating and any Sleaze
utility they're running (or half their Masking if they aren't). Whoever nets more successes wins;
a tie goes to the decker. *(SR3 p.207, p.209–210)*

entries.text: ## Security tally, alerts, and the Security Sheaf *(SR3 p.210–211)*

pdf.quote: A system's security sheaf lists the system's trigger steps

entries.text:
Every success the host scores against a decker — win or lose the contest — adds to that decker's
running **security tally** on that system, for as long as they stay logged on. A **security
sheaf** is the GM's plan for what that tally triggers: a list of thresholds ("trigger steps"),
each one arming some mix of IC and raising the system's **alert status**.

pdf.quote: Regardless of the test outcome, the gamemaster records
A system's security sheaf lists the system's trigger steps

entries.note: The tally is kept (every host success added); the sheaf's trigger steps are the GM's — not automated (TODO 128).

entries.text:
Systems start with **no alert**. Enough tally reaches a **passive alert**, which typically starts
throwing proactive IC at the decker and adds **+2 to every subsystem rating**; enough more reaches
an **active alert**, tightening things further. How dense the trigger steps are, and how much
tally each one takes, is entirely the GM's call — a high-security system stacks its triggers close
together, a relaxed one spreads them out.

entries.text:
A few in words: **Logon to Host/LTG/RTG** get you into a host or grid and start your security
tally there. **Locate** operations are "interrogations" — you can repeat them, narrowing your
search each time, to track down a file, a slave device, another decker, or IC. **Download/Upload
Data** and **Swap Memory** move data or programs and take real time to finish, running in the
background once started. **Control Slave**, **Edit Slave**, **Monitor Slave**, **Make Comcall**,
and **Tap Comcall** are "monitored" operations — you spend a Free Action every Initiative Pass to
keep them going, or they abort. **Graceful Logoff** is the clean way out, avoiding Dump Shock and
wiping your tracks; jacking out any other way risks it.

A world setting, **Matrix Ruleset** (in Foundry's Configure Settings), switches between
**"Matrix Defragged v2"** (the default) and **"Orthodox SR3 Matrix"** — this page's rules.
Changing it needs a full Foundry restart, and the GM sees a warning that switching mid-campaign
could break things, so it's a session-zero decision.

**Active/Storage Memory**, **I/O Speed**, and **Response** (Response Increase). A **Browse
Cyberdecks** button opens a picker over the system's cyberdeck compendium and loads a chosen
model's stats onto your sheet in one click. Your four persona programs — **Bod**, **Evasion**,
**Masking**, **Sensor** — are editable fields the sheet checks against your MPCP: it flags a
warning if any single program exceeds MPCP, or if they add up past three times MPCP. A **Sleaze**
rating field and a **Loaded Programs** list (each with its own rating and computed memory cost,
filled from a similar **Browse Programs** picker) round out your utilities. The sheet computes
your **Hacking Pool**, **Detection Factor**, and **Matrix Initiative** for you from these numbers.

entries.reason: heading

entries.text:
A **Log On To Host** control picks which host actor you're connected to (and resets your
security tally and alert level when you log on or off), and separate buttons set the host's
**alert level** — No Alert, Passive Alert, or Active Alert. A **Matrix Condition Monitor** — 10
clickable boxes, plus quick buttons for Light/Moderate/Serious/Deadly damage or healing one box —
tracks your icon's health; filling it triggers Dumpshock automatically: **Stun**, Power equal to
the connected host's Security Value, and a level from its Security Code (see Dump Shock above).

entries.reason: heading

entries.text:
A **System Test** button opens a dialog naming the connected host, your Computer skill and
Hacking Pool, your Detection Factor, and a dropdown to pick which subsystem — **Access, Control,

automatically if the host is on Passive Alert), and you can name the action and adjust the TN for
any utility you're running. Rolling it posts a two-sided chat card — your dice and TN on one side,
the host's Security Value and Detection Factor TN on the other — that resolves as a Success

**security tally**, regardless of who wins the overall contest.

entries.text: ### IC and the host sheet
entries.reason: heading

entries.text:
A host actor under this ruleset sets its **Security Code** (Blue/Green/Orange/Red/Black) and
**Alert** level (Passive/Active/Shutdown) at the top of its sheet, with its five **subsystem
ratings** and overall **Security Value** editable below. Its IC tab lists IC actors assigned to
it — each with a type drawn from a fixed roster of classic IC names, a Proactive/Reactive toggle,
and a note for which alert level deploys it — and a deploy button that brings assigned IC into the
current encounter. An IC actor's own sheet is mostly just a **Rating**; its attack pool and the
damage it can absorb both draw from its host's Security Value rather than from any stat of its
own, matching the book's treatment of IC as an extension of the host defending it.

entries.text: ### Dumpshock
entries.reason: heading

entries.text:
Beyond the automatic trigger when your Matrix Condition Monitor fills, a **Dumpshock** button on
the Matrix tab lets a GM or player fire it manually for any other reason the story calls for. Its
dialog takes the host's **Security Code** and **Security Value** (filled in from the connected host)
and posts the book's damage: **Stun**, Power equal to the Security Value, and a level from the Dump
Shock Damage Levels table (Blue Light, Green Moderate, Orange Serious, Red Deadly) — the same as the
automatic version. The resist card rolls **Willpower** with no armor (a house ruling: the book names
no attribute). Either way, the system only announces the damage; the GM still applies it.

> - The range table was invented. Grenades have **their own** range table,

>   per meter**. There is no "12D HE".

>   wave. It is not a series of separate damage rolls.

> - **Stun**: TN is **2 plus your injury modifiers**, not 2 plus the number of

>   base time is divided by your successes. The "nurse / hospital / DocWagon"
>   modifiers in the original were invented. The real ones are on the
>   Doctoring Table below.

entries.text: ### Riggers, jacking in, and Control Pool  *(SR3 p.44, p.130, p.140, p.301)*

pdf.quote: adds +2 to the user's Reaction and +1D6 Initiative dice while
Bonuses for boosted and wired reflexes,

entries.text:
A **rigger** carries a **Vehicle Control Rig (VCR)**, cyberware that lets
them drive a suitably wired vehicle through a neural link instead of a
wheel or yoke. Jacked in this way, a rigger gets several things an
ordinary driver doesn't:

pdf.quote: adds +2 to the user's Reaction and +1D6 Initiative dice while

entries.note: Introductory; the specifics are in the next units.

entries.text:
- **A better Initiative.** Each VCR level is worth **+2 Reaction and one
  extra Initiative die** while rigging *(SR3 p.301)*. This is a
  replacement, not a stack: wired reflexes, boosted reflexes, and magical
  or adept increases to Reaction or Initiative **do not apply** for a
  rigger determining Initiative this way *(SR3 p.140)*.

pdf.quote: adds +2 to the user's Reaction and +1D6 Initiative dice while
Bonuses for boosted and wired reflexes,

entries.text:
- **A Control Pool.** This works like Combat Pool or Spell Pool but is
  spent only on tests to control the rigged vehicle: driving, dodging
  incoming fire, and resisting collision damage. Its size is simply the
  rigger's own Reaction plus twice their VCR level — nothing else adds to
  it — and any single test can only draw as many Control Pool dice as it
  has base skill dice *(SR3 p.44)*. **No VCR means no Control Pool at
  all**, even for a rigger driving a vehicle they aren't currently jacked
  into.

pdf.quote: A rigger's Control Pool is equal to the character's Reaction,
modified only by his or her vehicle control rig (VCR) cyberware.

entries.text:
- **An easier default.** A VCR lets its user default to Reaction for any
  Vehicle Skill test at only **+2** to the target number, instead of the
  usual +4 for defaulting to an unrelated attribute *(SR3 p.301)*.

pdf.quote: to default to Reaction for any Vehicle Skill at a +2 modifier, as

entries.note: The guide itself says this is not modelled (TODO 106).

entries.text:
- Riggers can alternatively jack into a **remote control deck** to run
  drones from a distance instead of riding in them. Left with no driver at
  all, a drone falls back on its own **Pilot Rating** in place of a skill.

dice (up to their skill rating) instead of the autonav bonus, on top of
reducing the target number by their VCR level.

entries.text: ### Getting a vehicle onto a character's sheet
entries.reason: describes the system's interface, not a book rule

entries.text:
A vehicle is its own **actor**, with its own sheet (Stats / Weapons / Mods
/ Electronic Warfare / Notes tabs). To give a character a vehicle:
entries.reason: describes the system's interface, not a book rule

entries.text:
- **Drag the vehicle actor onto the character sheet.** Dragging a
  compendium vehicle **deploys a working copy** and sets that character as
  its driver; dragging an existing world vehicle **links** it to that
  character instead. Both routes run through the GM so the character ends
  up with **owner** permission on the new or linked vehicle actor, whether
  or not a Player has permission to create actors directly.
entries.reason: describes the system's interface, not a book rule

entries.text:
- Or, on the character sheet's **Vehicles** tab, click **+ Add Vehicle**,
  which opens the same dialog with three sources: link an existing world
  vehicle, create a blank one, or pull one from a compendium.
entries.reason: describes the system's interface, not a book rule

entries.text:
- The Vehicles tab lists every vehicle whose pilot is this character, with
  its Handling/Speed/Body/Armor/Pilot/Sensor at a glance, a link to open
  its sheet, and per-vehicle **VCR / RCD / Auto** mode buttons plus a ✕ to
  unlink it (the vehicle itself isn't deleted — it can be added back).
entries.reason: describes the system's interface, not a book rule

entries.text:
- On the vehicle's own sheet, the **Pilot** dropdown sets who drives it,
  and **Passengers** (add/remove tags in the header) tracks who else is
  aboard — this is the roster a crash or ram reaches, without needing a
  Chase Scene open.

### Driving without rigging, in Foundry
{: #driving-without-rigging-in-foundry }
entries.reason: heading

entries.text:
A character with no VCR item at all — the ordinary case — still uses the
same 🚗 Driving Test dialog described just below. The "Using VCR" option
in it only shows up once the system finds VCR cyberware on the driver;
without one, the pool simply builds as Vehicle Skill plus Autonav, with no
Control Pool line at all, since the underlying Control Pool calculation
returns zero for anyone without a VCR rating. The vehicle's control-mode
button is normally left on **RCD** for this case: mechanically, "no VCR
bonus" is one path whether the driver is remote-piloting a drone or simply
sitting behind the wheel, so the same Reaction-based Initiative and pool
math cover both, and the mode buttons are shared between them. Defaulting
with no matching Vehicle Skill opens the same Default Table dialog
described in the note above — it always offers the ordinary +4-to-an-
attribute default, with no special case for a rigger's +2.

entries.text: ### Dump shock, and rigger damage from a destroyed vehicle
entries.reason: heading

entries.text:
- **⚡ Dump Shock** is a button in the character sheet's *Rigger —
  Electronic Warfare* panel (and beside the Matrix tools when in VR). Its
  dialog asks what the character was dumped from: the Matrix (a decker),
  a **remote-control network**, which uses the RC deck Rating from the
  panel, or a **vehicle** they were jacked out of. The rigger cases post
  the book's Power, **(Rating + 4)S** or **5S** Stun. The resist card rolls
  **Willpower**, with no armor. The card also states the ten turns of
  **+2** disorientation and offers the **Willpower (4) Test** that
  shortens it; that roll's result card says how many Combat Turns it lasts.

entries.text: ### The Chase Scene (combat tracker)
entries.reason: heading

entries.text:
The 🚗 Chase Scene tool, opened from the Rollable Tables sidebar tab (open
to every player, not just the GM), implements the book's vehicle-combat
maneuver system rather than standing in for it with something simpler: it
tracks each participant's vehicle type, terrain and speed, computes their
Maneuver Score, and offers dedicated action buttons for Accel/Brake,
Positioning, Ramming, Hiding and Relocating, each opening a dialog with
the relevant modifiers pre-filled and live target-number and pool math.
One participant can be flagged **Quarry** — everyone else's distance is
then tracked relative to it (positive behind, negative ahead), and at the
end of each turn the tool updates every pursuer's distance from the speed
difference automatically, reporting who's closing and who's falling
behind. Driver Points get the same reroll-on-6 handling as every other
open-ended roll in the system.

entries.reason: heading

entries.text:
A vehicle actor typed as a drone works the same way as any other vehicle —
Pilot dropdown, VCR/RCD/Auto modes — except its natural state is Auto,

target number, with any Command-channel electronic-warfare degradation
folded in automatically. Zero successes means the drone does nothing
useful; one gets the order followed literally; two or more gives it some
leeway.

entries.text: ## Worked example: a ramming attempt
entries.reason: heading

entries.text:
Dex is jacked into his **step-van** (Handling 4, Body 8) with Car Skill 5
and a Rating-2 VCR, chasing a **patrol car** (Handling 4, Body 3) driven by
an unrigged cop with Car Skill 4. Dex's van is doing 96 meters a turn to
the patrol car's 60. For this Combat Turn, assume Dex's Maneuver Score
came out to 42 against the patrol car's 28 — a gap of more than 10 in
Dex's favor.
entries.reason: worked-example setup; states no rule

entries.text:
1. **Control Pool.** Reaction 5 plus twice his VCR level (2) gives Dex a
   Control Pool of 9 dice, though any one test can only draw up to his 5
   Car Skill dice from it.

pdf.quote: A rigger's Control Pool is equal to the character's Reaction,

entries.note: Reaction 5 + 2 × VCR 2 = 9, capped at Car 5 per test: checks.

entries.text:
2. **The Ramming Test.** Base target number is his van's Handling, 4. His
   Maneuver Score beats the patrol car's by more than 10 (−4); terrain is
   normal (0); his VCR knocks off a further 2 × his Rating 2 (−4). Total
   modifier −8 against a base of 4 gives a target number of −4, floored at
   the rule's minimum of 2. He rolls his 5 Car Skill dice (no Control Pool
   needed at this target number) and gets 3 successes: the ram connects.

pdf.quote: Attacker has a Level 2 VCR -4
The final Target Number is 3 - 8, or -5, which rounds

   in speed; divided by ten and rounded up, that's a Power of 4, landing
   as Moderate on the Impact Damage Levels Table (21–60 m/turn).

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> Original gist: "Cyberware Grades & Secondhand Gear Guide".
> - **Betaware is ×.6 Essence**, not ×.7.
> - **Used cyberware costs the Essence of its grade**, not ×1.25. It costs
>   **half price**, not ×.75.
> - The availability modifiers were invented. Alphaware is **as available as
>   basic**. Betaware is **+5 to the TN and ×1.5 the time**. Deltaware is at
>   least **+9 and ×3**. Used is standard.
> - **Betaware isn't available to starting characters** either, not only
>   deltaware.
> - Used deltaware **can't be bought**, but if you get hold of some, it can
>   be **installed as betaware**. It isn't "destroyed on extraction".
> - Used implants come with **1D3 permanent Stress Points**, not "1 to 2".
> - **Removing** chrome never gives Essence back. A *later* implant can use
>   the "Essence hole", but only through a surgical option at +2 Threshold.
> - The 1–3 hour harvest window, the TN 4–8 extraction roll and the
>   "Electronics (Cyberware) scrub" aren't in *Man & Machine*.

entries.text: ## Selling harvested chrome
entries.reason: section heading

entries.text:
*Man & Machine* has no separate resale rule for used implants, so sell them
the same way as any other loot. Use the [fencing rules](../gear-and-fencing/#fencing-the-loot)
*(SR3 p.237–238)*: a **30%** base, **5% per net success** on the
Negotiation, never below **10%** or above **50%**. Stolen chrome isn't
standard gear, so expect the Finding a Fence TN to rise.

pdf.quote: The base price for most loot is 30 percent of its actual value
If the team won, the payment price will not rise above 50 percent of the actual value

entries.note: Resale of harvested chrome goes through the fencing rules, which are not built (see gear-and-fencing.md #43-70). The example arithmetic checks: 2,500 + 11,500 = 14,000; 30% = 4,200; 10% = 1,400; 50% = 7,000.

spur** (11,500¥) *(SR3 p.302)* list at **14,000¥** together. The fence's

below 1,400¥ or above 7,000¥.

# Buying Gear & Fencing
{: .no_toc }
entries.reason: page title / description / table of contents / horizontal rule / index page

entries.text:
Availability, Street Index and Legality Codes; buying through contacts; and
selling stolen goods to a fence. All rules are from the core rulebook,
*(SR3 p.237–238, p.270–274)*.

pdf.quote: Availability is a measure of how easy it is to obtain the item on the street

entries.text:
1. TOC
{:toc}
entries.reason: page title / description / table of contents / horizontal rule / index page

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> Original gist: "Gear Availability, Acquisition, & Fencing Guide".
> - SR3 Legality Codes look like **`6P-E`**, not "R" or "F". The number is
>   the restriction level, **P** means a permit is available, and the letter
>   is the category.
> - Successes on the acquisition test **divide** the base time. They don't
>   cut it by 25–50% each.
> - Paying to hurry a search costs **+2 days and +0.1 Street Index for each
>   −1 to the Availability TN**. It's not "+25–50% per die".
> - The price is **negotiated**: Negotiation against Intelligence, **5% per
>   net success**.
> - Fencing: the **30% base and 5% per net success** were right, but the
>   limits are a **10% floor and a 50% ceiling**, not 60%. The "chop shop 10–15%"
>   rate and the hot, encrypted and scarce percentage modifiers were invented.
>   The book handles risk through the **Finding a Fence** TN instead.
> - The **Ares Predator III** isn't in the core rulebook. The examples below
>   use the core **Ares Predator** (450¥, Availability 3/24 hrs, Street
>   Index .5).

pdf.quote: Whichever side wins the Negotiation Test alters the price paid in his or her favor by 5 percent per extra success
If the fence won, the payment price will not drop below 10 percent of the actual value

entries.note: Composite errata callout. What is implemented (Availability as TN / base time, successes dividing the time, −1 TN for 2 days and +0.1 Street Index, negotiation at 5% per net success) is checked at #9, #16-20. Not implemented: Legality Codes (the 6P-E notation is not stored on any pack item) and fencing, whose 30% base, 5% per net success, 10% floor and 50% ceiling are at #43-70. The 'Ares Predator III is not in the core rulebook' claim is true (no such entry in the text).

entries.text: ## Reading a gear entry  *(SR3 p.270–272)*

pdf.quote: Each piece of gear has an individual description and a table listing

entries.text: | Statistic | Meaning |
entries.reason: table header row

entries.text: | **Concealability** | TN for Perception Tests to spot it. Searches use half. |

pdf.quote: Searches have a target number of half the regular Concealability Rating (rounding down)

entries.text: | **Availability** | Two numbers: **TN / base time**, for example `3/24 hrs`. |

pdf.quote: The number to the left is a target number that represents the difficulty of obtaining the item; the one to the right represents the base time necessary to acquire it

entries.text: | **Cost** | The legal retail price in nuyen. |

pdf.quote: Cost is the base cost of the weapon in nuyen

entries.text: | **Street Index** | The black-market multiplier on Cost. |

pdf.quote: Street Index is the market value multiplier to the item's base cost

entries.text: | **Legality** | Restriction level, permit availability, and category. |

pdf.quote: Legality represents whether or not it is illegal to own the item, carry or transport it, what restriction category it falls into, and whether or not permits for the item are available

entries.note: A legality text field exists on a few item types (drugs, one other), but Legality Codes are not stored on weapons and gear and nothing interprets them.

entries.text:
At character creation, no gear may have a Device Rating above **6** or an
Availability above **8**. *(SR3 p.270)* Gear modified for a dwarf costs
**+10%**, and for a troll **+25%**. *(SR3 p.272)*

pdf.quote: no character may start the game with a piece of gear whose Availability is greater than 8

entries.note: The dwarf +10% / troll +25% surcharge is implemented (purchasing.mjs RACIAL_SURCHARGE). The character-creation limits (Device Rating at most 6, Availability at most 8) are not enforced.

entries.text: ## Buying on the street  *(SR3 p.272–273)*

pdf.quote: characters must use an appropriate contact

entries.text:
1. **Find a source.** Contact a fixer or other suitable contact and make an
   **Etiquette Test** against the **Availability TN**. Contacts differ: a
   talismonger is great for magical goods and poor for guns.

pdf.quote: the player gets in touch with a contact (usually a fixer) and makes an Etiquette Test
Talismongers, for example, are an ideal contact for magical items, but not very good at acquiring weapons

code.snippet: talismonger:  { good: ['focus', 'spell', 'magical'], bad: ['firearm', 'melee', 'projectile', 'ammunition'], note: 'ideal for magical items, poor for weapons (p.272)' },

entries.text:
2. **Wait.** **Base time ÷ successes** is how long it takes the source to
   find the item.

pdf.quote: The base time divided by the number of successes provides the actual time it takes the source to locate the item

entries.text:
3. **No successes?** The contact can't or won't find it. At the GM's
   discretion you can put the word out: **for each −1 to the Availability
   TN, add 2 days to the wait and +0.1 to the Street Index**. *(SR3 p.273)*

pdf.quote: the character may add 2 days to the acquisition time period and .1 to the Street Index (increasing the cost) in order to reduce the Availability target number by 1

code.snippet: export const REDUCTION = { daysPerPoint: 2, streetIndexPerPoint: 0.1, page: 'SR3 p.272' };

entries.text:
4. **Negotiate.** Halfway through the wait you meet the source. The asking
   price is **Cost × Street Index**, plus any increase from step 3. You and
   the source each roll **Negotiation against the other's Intelligence**.
   The winner moves the price **5% per net success** in their favor.
   *(SR3 p.273)*

pdf.quote: Halfway through this period, face-to-face negotiations to determine the actual cost take place
pitting their Negotiations Skill Ratings against each other's Intelligence

code.snippet: return { time, halfway: time / 2, found: true };

entries.text:
5. **Pick up.** If you won't pay, the deal is off, and the GM may raise the
   Availability TN next time you use that contact. *(SR3 p.273)*

pdf.quote: gamemasters can adjust the Availability target number upward the next time the character searches for something through that contact

entries.note: The deal being off if you won't pay is a card nobody presses (nothing is charged until 💴). Raising the Availability TN for that contact next time is not tracked.

entries.text: ### The book's example  *(SR3 p.273)*

pdf.quote: She wants to buy it on the street. The whip has an Availability of 24/14 days, with a Street Index of 3

entries.text:
Cheshire wants a **monofilament whip**: Availability **24/14 days**,
Street Index **3**, Cost **3,000¥**. None of her contacts come close to TN

pdf.quote: That means she'll be waiting 24 extra days (2 x 12 = 24)
That makes the cost a whopping 12,600

entries.text:
24. She puts the word out, cutting the TN to **12**. That adds **24 days**
(2 × 12) and **+1.2** Street Index. She rolls 2 successes: (24 + 14) ÷ 2 =
**19 days**. The price is 3,000 × 4.2 = **12,600¥**. She wins the
negotiation by 4, which is 20% off, and pays **10,080¥**.

pdf.quote: That means she'll be waiting 24 extra days (2 x 12 = 24)
That makes the cost a whopping 12,600

like, and how fake IDs work in SR3.

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> Original gist: "Life with a SIN vs. Living SINless".
> - The **Fake SIN price table was invented**. In SR3 a fake ID is a forged
>   credstick, and its rating sets its price: **Rating × Rating × 1,000¥** at
>   ratings 1–4, rising steeply after that. The table is below.
> - A SIN is not a "12-digit alphanumeric code". The book says the number is
>   **generated from personal data**, and police can read your birth date,
>   state of origin and initials from it.
> - "30–40% of the population is SINless" appears in no SR3 book checked.
> - There's no "Lesser / Greater Magical Permit". In the UCAS and CAS, magic
>   of **Force 3 or more** is regulated and needs a permit. Unregistered
>   spells, spirits and foci fall under legality category **(T) Class E
>   Magic**.
> - Permits **require a valid SIN**, and a fake one must beat a Rating 6
>   verification system.

pdf.quote: Availability Rating/24 hours Rating/72 hours Rating/14 days Rating/30 days Street Index 1 1 1 1
The actual numbers that compose a SIN are generated by a complex formula from several pieces of personal data
If using a fake ID (see p. 239) to purchase a permit, the ID must beat a Rating 6 verification system in an Opposed Test

entries.note: Composite errata callout. Checked against the book: a forged credstick's price is Rating × Rating × 1,000¥ at ratings 1-4 (p.239) and rises after that; SIN numbers are generated from personal data (p.238); Force 3+ magic is regulated with permits (MitS p.11); Class E Magic covers unregistered spells, spirits and foci (p.274); permits need a valid SIN and a fake must beat a Rating 6 system (p.274). The '30-40% of the population is SINless' claim is an absence claim I did not search for. None of this is modelled in the system.

- The **UCAS** introduced SINs in **2036**, requiring every citizen to
  register. People living in the UCAS without one are "probationary
  citizens": they can't vote and have few or no civil rights.

entries.text: ## Life with a SIN  *(SR3 p.238–239)*
entries.reason: Section heading citing SR3 pp.238-239, over background text about SINs and credsticks with no mechanical counterpart in the system.

entries.text:
You need a SIN to get a legal job, open a bank account, own property, go to
school, rent an apartment, set up utilities, and travel legally, which
includes **buying a bus ticket**. Your credstick carries your ID, licenses
and permits, and can hold your fingerprints, palmprints and retinal prints.
entries.reason: Background / lore about SINs and credsticks (printed pp.238-239); no code counterpart. entries.text:
The cost is a **data trail**. Every legal purchase leaves credit records and
inventory, and possibly video footage, and stores that realize they sold to
shadowrunners will hand those records to the police. *(SR3 p.273)*

databases all over the world. Only well-connected forgery outfits, often
based in data havens, can do it. At least **half the cost is paid up
front** to the fixer.

- In the UCAS and CAS, **any spell, spirit, focus or other magical effect of
  Force 3 or higher is legally regulated**, though permits can be had. A
  felony committed with magic always counts as **premeditated**. *(MitS p.11)*
